concepts.title: The Mahabharata as a Dynamic Text
concepts.section: The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata
concepts.definition: The Mahabharata, attributed to Vyasa, grew over roughly a thousand years of composition, and its critical edition - prepared over 47 years by the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute project - compared Sanskrit versions from across the subcontinent to reconstruct the most ancient core of about 100,000 verses.
concepts.key_idea: A text that kept growing shows a society that kept debating itself: the epic's variants are evidence, not noise.

solution_steps.explain: the critical edition compared manuscripts to recover the oldest recoverable text

concepts.title: Varna and Jati in Social Order
concepts.definition: Brahmanical theory ranked society into four varnas - brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra - with duties assigned by birth, while practice showed jatis as flexible occupational communities whose hierarchies varied by region; texts like the Dharmasutras policed boundaries, and non-conforming groups were marked as untouchable.
concepts.key_idea: Varna was the ideal map, jati the lived terrain: the gap between them is where social history happens.

solution_steps.explain: birth-fixed duties for four varnas claim divine origin

concepts.title: Patriliny, Gender and Marriage
concepts.definition: Epic and dharmashastric norms idealised patriliny - descent through sons - with the Mahabharata's core story defending it; texts debated women's property (stridhana), prescribed wives' subordination to husbands, and recorded alternative systems like matriliny hints and younger brothers marrying widows among some communities.
concepts.key_idea: The preference for sons structured inheritance, ritual and emotion - and the texts show both enforcement and anxiety about it.

concepts.title: Beyond Varna: Kings, Workers and Others
concepts.definition: The chapter follows social differences into practice: kings claimed kshatriya status even when of varied origins, artisans and workers shaped urban economies, and Tamilakam's sangam texts describe society with different categories, showing that varna never exhaustively described Indian society.
concepts.key_idea: Wherever the sources let us look - guild inscriptions, sangam poems, palli donations - society proves more layered than the fourfold schema.
